"executive_summary": "This work reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics performed at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. The authors use the common, low-cost organic photocatalyst Eosin Y (EY) together with K3PO4 as base and CTAB as the surfactant that forms positively charged micelles. Through photophysical studies, they establish that EY binds preferentially to CTAB micelles (EY@CTAB) via electrostatic interactions, since EY carries two negative charges at pH 7 and interacts with the positively charged CTAB. The micellar scaffold solubilizes both the hydrophobic arylamine substrates and the photocatalyst at the Stern layer, bringing them into close proximity for a bimolecular reaction. The optimized reaction converts p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene with 100% conversion within 4 h using only 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equivalents of K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB, triggered by green light (λ = 525 nm) under ambient air. This is a dramatic improvement over the previous Ir-based method, which gave only 64% conversion after 24 h in bulk acetonitrile. The authors attribute the boosting to non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps, as revealed by fluorescence up-conversion measurements, and to the modulation of redox potentials at the CAI. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps in the presence of p-anisidine. Radical trap experiments using BHT confirm the formation of amine radicals, and control experiments with H2O2 sensing strips demonstrate that atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, being reduced to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) to regenerate the photocatalyst. The methodology shows a broad substrate scope, achieving 100% conversion with electron-rich arylamines and 98% and 95% with p-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline, respectively. The authors emphasize that this is the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds and claim that their approach outperforms all previously reported catalytic methodologies. This work opens newer opportunities in the synthesis of azoaromatics and represents a green, sustainable alternative to traditional diazotization and metal-catalyzed routes. The study is notable for its emphasis on sustainability, ambient conditions, and the use of a common, inexpensive photocatalyst, positioning it as a significant advance in green organic synthesis.",

summary.title: Metal-Free Photocatalysis at Charged Aqueous Interface: Boosting the Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Arylamines to Azoaromatics under Ambient Conditions
summary.authors: Shivendra Singh; Vidhi Agarwal; Tridib K Sarma; Tushar Kanti Mukherjee
summary.executive_summary: This work reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics performed at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. The authors formulate a green protocol that uses the micellar surface as a scaffold to co-host the organic photocatalyst Eosin Y (EY) and the arylamine substrates, enabling a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps. The reaction proceeds in water with only 0.6 mol% EY, K3PO4 as base, and 40 mM cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), completing in 4 h with up to 100% conversion and 100% selectivity. The authors argue that the dramatic boost in catalytic efficacy arises from the non-diffusive PET and the modulation of redox potentials at the CAI, which brings the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity within the micellar Stern layer. This approach is presented as the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds and as a more sustainable alternative to prior metal-catalyzed and Ir-based photocatalytic methods, which suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high catalyst doses, and the need for inert atmospheres. The study demonstrates a broad substrate scope spanning electron-rich and electron-deficient amine centers, with products characterized by GC-MS and NMR. The authors position this methodology as opening new opportunities in the synthesis of azoaromatics for applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial processes. The paper is a preprint hosted on ChemRxiv under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license and is not peer-reviewed. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics performed at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. The authors formulate a green protocol that uses the micellar surface as a scaffold to co-host the organic photocatalyst Eosin Y (EY) and the arylamine substrates, enabling a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps. The reaction proceeds in water with only 0.6 mol% EY, K3PO4 as base, and 40 mM cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), completing in 4 h with up to 100% conversion and 100% selectivity. The authors argue that the dramatic boost in catalytic efficacy arises from the non-diffusive PET and the modulation of redox potentials at the CAI, which brings the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity within the micellar Stern layer. This approach is presented as the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds and as a more sustainable alternative to prior metal-catalyzed and Ir-based photocatalytic methods, which suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high catalyst doses, and the need for inert atmospheres. The study demonstrates a broad substrate scope spanning electron-rich and electron-deficient amine centers, with products characterized by GC-MS and NMR. The authors position this methodology as opening new opportunities in the synthesis of azoaromatics for applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial processes. The paper is a preprint hosted on ChemRxiv under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license and is not peer-reviewed. The bibliography is not provided in the supplied text, so top_influential_citations is set to an empty string. The study is conducted without reported human or animal subjects, so ethical considerations are not applicable. The paper does not report data or code availability statements, so those fields are set to empty strings.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are important functional organic molecules with applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and industry. Traditional azo synthesis relies on diazotization with stoichiometric nitrile salts, producing unstable diazonium intermediates and waste. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed and Ir-based photocatalytic methods exist but suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, and inert atmospheres. Photocatalytic oxidative coupling with O2 is attractive but prior arylamine-to-azo methods use organic solvents and limited catalysts. Charged aqueous interfaces can modulate photochemical reactions via confinement and unique electric fields. A green aqueous route for azo synthesis at ambient conditions remains an important unmet goal.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a metal-free, aqueous, ambient photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics can be achieved efficiently. The hypothesis is that charged aqueous interfaces of micelles can boost catalytic efficacy via non-diffusive PET and redox potential modulation. It is predicted that EY will associate selectively with CTAB micelles due to electrostatic interactions between its negative charges and CTAB. It is predicted that PET will be ultrafast, with a time constant on the order of picoseconds. It is predicted that the reaction will proceed with high conversion, selectivity, and low catalyst loading under ambient air. It is predicted that atmospheric O2 will act as a sacrificial oxidant, being reduced to H2O2 to regenerate the photocatalyst.

Methodological Details
The study investigates metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics in aqueous medium. The authors use Eosin Y (EY) as the organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as the base. The reaction is carried out at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. Three surfactants are screened: cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and triton X-100 (TX-100). EY shows a bathochromic shift of 9 and 16 nm in the presence of CTAB and TX-100 micelles, respectively. EY exhibits enhanced fluorescence of 2.4-fold only in the presence of CTAB at and near the critical micellar concentration. No spectral changes are observed for EY in the presence of SDS, signifying lack of interaction. EY bears two negative charges at pH 7 and interacts electrostatically with the positively charged CTAB. The enhanced fluorescence lifetime of EY rises from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. The reaction uses 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. CTAB forms spherical micelles at an optimized concentration of 40 mM, as revealed from HR-TEM measurements. The model substrate is p-anisidine, converted to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene. Conversion is determined from GC-MS measurements, and products are characterized by GC-MS and NMR. The reaction is triggered by green light at a wavelength of 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. The reaction completes within 4 h to give 100% conversion to the desired azo product. K3PO4 neither interferes with EY-CTAB association nor interacts with the excited state of EY@CTAB. Arylamines prefer to solubilize at the less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous interface of the micellar Stern layer. Both the substrate and the photocatalyst remain solubilized inside the micellar scaffold.

Procedures And Architectures
The methodology is based on the specific association of substrate and photocatalyst with the micellar assembly. Photophysical behavior of EY is studied in the presence of CTAB, SDS, and TX-100. Micellar association is probed via absorption peak shifts and fluorescence quenching. Fluorescence lifetime is measured to confirm micellar association, rising from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns. Reaction optimization is tabulated in Table 1, using green light at 525 nm under ambient air. The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. The reaction achieves 100% conversion within 4 h with 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. Micelle morphology is confirmed as spherical at 40 mM via HR-TEM measurements. The reaction requires a base because proton abstraction is a critical step for POC of amine substrates. Inorganic bases K3PO4 and KOH, and organic base DABCO, are all effective, though DABCO gives slightly lower yields. Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, being reduced to H2O2 to regenerate the photocatalyst. H2O2 formation is detected with H2O2 sensing strips, showing color change before and after light irradiation. Fluorescence quenching is monitored at 545 nm upon addition of increasing concentrations of p-anisidine. A linear Stern-Volmer plot gives a quenching rate constant (kq) of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. The SV plot indicates a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process. Lack of fluorescence quenching with p-nitroaniline suggests no electron transfer to EY*@CTAB. K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots, signifying that PET precedes proton abstraction. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. Radical trap experiments use 2,6-di-tert-buty-4-methylphenol (BHT) to trap amine radicals. The reaction mixture is irradiated with green light for 5 min, then BHT is added and irradiated for 4 h. Products are analyzed using HR-MS and GC-MS measurements. A characteristic HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adducts appears at a molecular weight of 342.2399 g/mol. The presence of BHT results in negligible conversion of about 5.0% to the desired azo product.

Key Results
The optimized reaction gives 100% conversion to the azo product within 4 h under ambient air. The reaction uses only 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. Conversion is determined from GC-MS measurements, and CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM. The efficacy is enhanced with an 8.3-fold lower dose of EY compared to the previous report. The enhancement occurs only in the presence of CTAB micelles, indicating the critical role of the micellar environment. The reaction is feasible with blue light, but requires 6 h for 100% conversion under standard conditions. The reaction is feasible only in the presence of a base, as proton abstraction is a critical step. Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, being reduced to H2O2 to regenerate the photocatalyst. H2O2 formation is detected with H2O2 sensing strips, showing color change before and after light irradiation. Arylamines with electron-rich amine centers show 100% conversion within 4 h. This is remarkable compared to the previously reported 64% conversion after 24 h in bulk acetonitrile. Aniline shows 100% conversion under standard conditions as substrate 8. p-Chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline show conversion yields of 98% and 95%, respectively. The broad substrate scope includes electron-rich and electron-deficient amine centers. The quenching rate constant (kq) is 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, indicating a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process. Lack of fluorescence quenching with p-nitroaniline suggests no electron transfer to EY*@CTAB. K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots, signifying that PET precedes proton abstraction. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. The p-anisidine-BHT adduct appears at a molecular weight of 342.2399 g/mol in HR-MS. The presence of BHT results in negligible conversion of about 5.0% to the desired azo product. The mapped redox potentials indicate that oxidation of arylamines by EY* is thermodynamically feasible at the micellar surface.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The boost in catalytic efficacy arises mainly from non-diffusive PET and modulation of redox potentials at the CAI. The micellar surface acts as an efficient scaffold to host both EY and arylamines. The non-diffusive PET enables fast kinetics, completing the reaction in 4 h. The CAI brings the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity for bimolecular reactions. The interfacial surface charges dictate the interaction with the charged molecules. The approach outperforms all previously reported catalytic methodologies. The methodology is presented as the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds. The work opens newer opportunities in the synthesis of azoaromatics. The approach is sustainable, using a common and low-cost organic photocatalyst, Eosin Y. The reaction proceeds under ambient air, avoiding the need for inert atmospheres. The approach uses sustainable O2 as the oxidant, reducing waste compared to diazotization. The study suggests potential applications in optical storage and molecular switches. The study does not report mechanistic models beyond the PET and redox potential modulation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a preprint hosted on ChemRxiv and is explicitly not peer-reviewed. The reaction requires a base, as proton abstraction is a critical step for POC of amine substrates. The reaction is feasible only in the presence of a base, indicating a requirement that limits generality. The reaction is feasible with blue light, but requires 6 h for 100% conversion under standard conditions. The quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1 exceeds the diffusion limit, indicating a non-diffusive process. The exact value of the quenching rate constant appears to be truncated in the text. The text is truncated before the substrate scope details and mechanistic discussion.
